status_legend.published: a number printed by the named source (a maker, a standard, a peer-reviewed paper or a trade association)
status_legend.secondary: a number from a reference site or textbook that does not show its own primary source
status_legend.derived: computed here from published inputs (formula and inputs named); not itself published anywhere
status_legend.practice: a designer's or forum's rule of thumb, not a measurement
status_legend.speculation: a reasoned guess with no direct measurement behind it; do not treat as established

hazenWilliams_psiPer100ft.note: Irrigation Association 2008 friction-loss charts (reproduced in the Hunter handbook) and every Rain Bird / Spears chart use exactly this form; 0.2083... gives ft of head per 100 ft, x 0.433 converts to psi. Hunter writes the per-foot form hf = 0.00090194*(100/C)^1.852*Q^1.852/d^4.866*L.
hazenWilliams_psiPer100ft.check: 1 in Class 200 PVC (d=1.169), 10 gpm, C=150 gives 1.42 psi/100 ft; the IA chart prints 1.42 (Hunter handbook) -- the formula reproduces the charts.

velocity.note: ft/s from gpm and in. Charts shade V > 5 ft/s 'use with caution' (surge).

darcyWeisbach.expr: hf_ft = f * (L/D) * V^2/(2g); f from Colebrook (or Swamee-Jain); psi = 0.433 * ft
darcyWeisbach.note: 0.0015 mm is the usual 'drawn tubing / smooth plastic' value; the LibreTexts microirrigation table uses e = 0.0005 in (0.0127 mm) for PE; 0.15 mm (0.006 in) is the usual galvanized-iron value (secondary, Engineering ToolBox / pipeflow listings). Kinematic viscosity of water: 1.41e-5 ft2/s at 50 F, 1.22e-5 at 60 F, 1.06e-5 at 70 F.

minorLossK.expr: dp_psi = K * V^2/(2g) * 0.433 (V in the pipe, ft/s; V^2/2g in ft); equivalent length Le = K * D / f
minorLossK.note: An equivalent length in ft is only exact at the friction factor it was derived with; at the low Reynolds numbers of residential zones (Re 3,000-30,000) f is 0.025-0.045, so a fixed-ft table and a fixed-K table disagree by up to ~1.5x. The 2-K method (Hooper 1981) handles this: K = K1/Re + Kinf*(1 + 1/D_in).

suddenContractionExpansion.expr: contraction K = 0.5*(1 - beta^2); expansion K = (1 - beta^2)^2; both on the SMALL-bore velocity; beta = d_small/d_large; refer to pipe velocity by dividing by beta^4
suddenContractionExpansion.note: Textbook Borda-Carnot / Crane-style relations (sharp edges). Used below to DERIVE insert-fitting losses.

orificeNozzle.expr: q = 29.82 * Cd * D^2 * sqrt(P); in ratio form q2 = q1 * (P2/P1)^x with x = 0.5
orificeNozzle.note: LibreTexts (Irrigation Systems Management) defines P as 'pressure of the water at the inlet to the sprinkler device' and gives Cd about 0.96 for straight-bore nozzles.

industryStandard.summary: YES for PVC: C = 150 is the irrigation industry's design value. The Irrigation Association 2008 charts (Hunter handbook), Rain Bird's current and 2018 charts, Spears and Toro all print C=150 for Sch 40, Class 160/200/315 PVC. For polyethylene the same industry charts use C = 140, NOT 150 (IA 'PE 3408 ASTM D2239 C=140', Rain Bird 'SDR 7, 9, 11.5, 15 C=140', Toro/Hunter design C 140). PEX: C=150 (plumbing industry, PPFA). Copper: the irrigation charts use 140; the Copper Development Association and NFPA 13 use 150. Steel: the irrigation charts use C = 100 for Schedule 40 steel (a design/aged value).

values.what: design value, all irrigation charts and AWWA M23
Hunter handbook table 'Roughness coefficient C values' (same table as Toro's)

values.C: 155 (12 in) and 159 (6 in) new; 164.2 and 163.3 on 8 in pipe in service since 1976 (46 years)
values.what: Uni-Bell / Utah State Water Research Lab tests, 2022 (industry-funded; large municipal pipe, not 1/2-1 in)
IPEX bulletin citing experimental data; AWWA M23 still recommends 150

pvc.aging: No measured loss of C with age was found for PVC; the only in-service test (46 years, 8 in, municipal water) measured C > 160. Uni-Bell is the PVC trade association, so this is industry data.
pvc.hardWater: NO quantitative study of calcium-carbonate scale in PVC irrigation pipe was found. The Russian corrosion literature (Kamerstein, via Shcherbakov & Cuong) states that deposit and corrosion growth 'are not affected in plastic' pipes. A lateral that stays full of hard water between cycles can still scale at heads and fittings; treat any C below 150 for hard water as speculation.
pvc.iron: PVC does not rust. Iron-rich well water (iron bacteria / ochre slime) coats any pipe; extension sources give >0.1 ppm Fe as a drip-clogging risk, >0.3 ppm as staining, >1 ppm as an iron-bacteria risk. No C value for slimed PVC was found.

values.what: IA 2008 chart 'Polyethylene Plastic Pipe ID Controlled, PE 3408 ASTM D2239 C=140'; Rain Bird PE chart 'SDR 7, 9, 11.5, 15 C=140'
Hunter/Toro C table
Moghazi (1998), laboratory: C rises with diameter; fixed 130/140 gave errors up to 27%
IPEX lists 'Plastic (PVC & HDPE) 150' (from Karassik Pump Handbook)

pe_polyethylene_sidr.disagreement: Irrigation charts use 140; IPEX/Pump Handbook use 150 for HDPE; Moghazi measured 129-148 depending on size. For 3/4-1 in SIDR (19-27 mm ID) 140-148 is supported; for 1/2 in (15.8 mm ID) 135 is closer to Moghazi.

values.what: PPFA/NAHB Residential PEX design guide friction tables: 'Friction Loss based on Hazen-Williams Formula (C = 150)'

pex.aging: PPFA: 'PEX pipe does not corrode, and it is resistant to mineral build-up' (a claim, no C-vs-age data).
pex.hardWater: Claimed resistant to mineral build-up (PPFA); no measurement found.

values.what: IA 2008 Type K/L/M copper charts (ASTM B88 C=140) and Rain Bird Type K chart
Hunter/Toro C table ('Copper, Brass')
Copper Development Association's sizing calculator / Copper Tube Handbook (C = 150); NFPA 13 copper tube 150
Engineering ToolBox / Wikipedia table

copper_k_l_m.disagreement: 150 (CDA, NFPA 13) vs 140 (irrigation charts) vs 130 (Hunter/Toro 'design'). Use 140 new; 130 for old tube or hard water (Hunter's design value is the only aged-style number found).
copper_k_l_m.hardWater: Copper scales in hard water; no measured C-vs-age for small copper tube was found. Hunter/Toro's design C 130 (vs 140 new) is the only published allowance.
copper_k_l_m.iron: Not applicable to the tube; iron-bearing water deposits as in any pipe.

values.what: NFPA 13: galvanized steel, all system types (fire sprinklers)
Engineering ToolBox / Wikipedia 'galvanized iron 120' (no age given)
IA 2008 and Rain Bird Schedule 40 steel friction charts (ASTM A53, C=100) -- the irrigation industry's design value for steel
Hunter/Toro C table, 'Welded steel' (not galvanized specifically)
LibreTexts irrigation text, 'Galvanized steel pipe 140' (vs 'Standard steel pipe 100') -- an outlier, probably new irrigation-grade galvanized
pipeflowlab (cites Moody 1944 and Crane TP-410; could not verify against those)
a DIY calculator site, no age band, low authority -- the only source found for the '80-100' figure

ageBands.note: NO published C-by-age table for galvanized steel was found. The age bands that exist are for unlined CAST IRON and are often borrowed as a proxy: new 130; 10 yr 107-113; 20 yr 89-100; 30 yr 75-90; 40 yr 64-83 (Engineering ToolBox; Wikipedia copies it). EN 12845 uses C=100 for cast iron 'roughly a 20-year-old pipe' (Canute, secondary). Applying them to galvanized is SPECULATION.

waterChemistry.note: The mechanism is roughness growth (tubercles, scale) AND loss of bore. Kamerstein's classification (Russian literature, for steel and cast-iron mains) gives annual growth of absolute roughness by water group: 1 low-corrosion 0.005-0.05 mm/yr (avg 0.025); 2 moderate, organic matter and dissolved iron < 3 g/m3, 0.055-0.18 (avg 0.07); 3 significant, iron > 3 g/m3, 0.18-0.4 (avg 0.20); 4 strong, high sulfates/chlorides, 0.4-0.6 (avg 0.51); 5 very strong, 'significant carbonate' and highly mineralized, 0.6-3.0 mm/yr. The paper's C-vs-age tables are for 250 and 400 mm mains (e.g. group 1, 250 mm, e0 0.3 mm: 127.9 at 5 yr, 109.4 at 20, 83.8 at 40).
waterChemistry.smallPipeWarning: In a 3/4 in (21 mm) pipe the same mm of growth is ~12x larger relative to the bore than in a 250 mm main, so a residential galvanized line ages far faster in C terms, and the bore itself closes. DERIVED illustration (Colebrook, 60 F, 4 gpm in 0.824 in pipe): e = 0.15 mm new -> C_equiv ~ 119; e = 0.15 + 20 yr x 0.025 = 0.65 mm -> C_equiv ~ 94; e = 0.15 + 20 yr x 0.07 = 1.55 mm -> C_equiv ~ 76, before any loss of bore. Treat as speculation: the growth rates are for mains.
waterChemistry.hardWater: Sources disagree on direction: moderately hard water can lay a protective calcium/zinc carbonate film that slows zinc loss (slower corrosion), but the scale itself narrows the bore. Net effect depends on chemistry (Langelier/stability index); no residential measurement found.
waterChemistry.iron: Iron in the water (Kamerstein groups 2-3) and iron bacteria accelerate tuberculation; once the zinc is gone, steel corrodes internally (tuberculation), which is the usual functional failure of galvanized water lines (secondary sources, 40-70 yr service life).

materials.temperature: Hazen-Williams has no viscosity term. The IA 2008 chart notes: 'Head loss decreases (increases) approximately 1% for every 3 F above (below) the reference temperature (73.4 F)'. Hunter/Toro tables are for 60 F / 50 F water. Engineering ToolBox limits H-W to 40-75 F water.

darcyVsHazenWilliams.irrigationReferencesPrefer: For SMALL smooth plastic pipe the agricultural/micro-irrigation references prefer Darcy-Weisbach: 'For small-diameter, smooth-walled pipe used in microirrigation (e.g., laterals), the Hazen-Williams equation with a C value of 150 underestimates the friction loss (Keller and Bliesner, 1990). They recommend the Darcy-Weisbach equation' (LibreTexts, quoting Keller & Bliesner). Allen (1996, Applied Eng. in Agric. 12:685-693) shows the H-W C is not a constant but varies with Reynolds number and velocity. Moghazi (1998) measured C rising from 129 to 148 as PE diameter rose 13 -> 22 mm. The landscape makers (Rain Bird, Hunter, Toro, IA) nonetheless publish only H-W charts for 1/2-6 in pipe.

derivedComparison.method: Colebrook with e = 0.0015 mm (smooth), water at 60 F (nu = 1.217e-5 ft2/s), compared with H-W C=150 on the same ID; C_equiv is the H-W C that would give the Darcy-Weisbach loss.
derivedComparison.reading: At residential lateral flows in 1/2-1 in smooth pipe (Re 5,000-30,000) Darcy-Weisbach behaves like H-W with C = 130-145, i.e. H-W C=150 under-predicts by ~5-25%, the gap largest at the lowest flows (where the absolute loss is smallest). The PE charts' C=140 lands near Darcy-Weisbach for 3/4-1 in at 4-8 gpm. Below Re ~4,000 (e.g. <1 gpm in 1 in pipe) flow is laminar/transitional and neither formula is reliable, but the loss there is negligible.

insideDiameters.note: Two ID conventions are in circulation for OD-controlled pipe (PVC, steel): (a) the IA 2008 'average ID' = OD - 2 x average wall (average wall = minimum wall + half the wall tolerance), used by the Hunter handbook and Rain Bird's current (2021) charts; (b) OD - 2 x MINIMUM wall, used by Rain Bird's older (2018) Class 200 chart and Hunter's older charts (TAMU copy). (b) is ~0.02 in larger, which is ~11% less friction at 3/4 in. Use (a): it is the IA's and the newer charts'. ID-controlled pipe (PE SIDR) has the same nominal ID at every SIDR; copper and PEX are CTS.

pvc_sch40.pressureNote: pressurePsi: Hunter handbook rating at 73.4 F, rounded; not for threaded pipe.

1/2.note: Class 200 is NOT made in 1/2 in (wall would be < 0.060 in min); charts substitute Class 315 (SDR 13.5)

pe_sidr.note: ID-controlled: SIDR-15, -11.5, -9 and -7 share the SAME nominal ID; only the wall/OD changes. Rain Bird's chart is headed 'SDR 7, 9, 11.5, 15' with one ID row.

pressureRating.note: DERIVED: this is why 'SIDR-15' is sold as both 80 psi (older PE 2306/3306 compounds) and 100 psi (PE 3408/4710). D2239-12a(2020) dropped the 2306/3306/3408 designations.

pex_sdr9_cts.standard: ASTM F876/F877, SDR 9, copper tube size
pex_sdr9_cts.note: IDs from PPFA Table 3.1 (average OD and average wall per ASTM F876); PPFA's own friction table uses 0.863 for 1 in.

galvanized_sch40.note: New-pipe ID. Old galvanized loses bore to tuberculation/scale; no published residential shrinkage figure was found.

values.note: spec text 'nominal inside diameter of 0.487 in', headline 0.49 in; wall 0.098 in; LLDPE; 80 psi; '8 gpm maximum'
FLEXsg 'Meets ASTM D2104, D2239, D2737'; SJ 150 psi
OD 0.70, wall 0.10, 120 psi; Toro sells it as '3/8 in'

swingPipe_funnyPipe.note: Swing pipe is NOT SIDR pipe: 0.49 in ID vs 0.622 for 1/2 in SIDR.

spears.what: 'Average Friction Loss for PVC and CPVC Fittings in Equivalent Feet of Straight Run Pipe' (Spears; Sch 40 basis)

hunterHandbook_plasticIPSorCopper.what: 'Table of approximate pressure losses for pipe fittings', 'Plastic IPS or Copper' rows; Hunter: use 'only when the manufacturer's recommended pressure loss values are not available'

ell45.note: the PDF's text layer reads 'Elbow, 34 deg' (typo or glyph error); taken as 45 deg, matching the steel table's row order

hunterOlderChart_standardSteelPipe.what: Hunter friction-loss charts (TAMU copy): 'Equivalent Length in Feet of Standard Steel Pipe'

pvc_solventWeld_equivalentFt.disagreement: Hunter's 2019 handbook 'Plastic IPS' values are ~2x Spears/Engineering ToolBox (3/4 in 90 ell 4.5 ft vs 2.0 ft; branch 9.0 vs 4.9). Spears is a PVC fitting maker; Hunter's table is generic. No source gives a coupling for PVC other than Hunter (1.5-4 ft); a solvent-weld coupling has a socket the size of the pipe OD and adds only a small step, so Hunter's coupling value is probably conservative (speculation).
pvc_solventWeld_equivalentFt.male_adapter: Only Engineering ToolBox lists a male/female adapter (1.0 / 1.5 / 2.0 ft at 1/2 / 3/4 / 1 in). Note the thread end of an MPT adapter is a smaller bore than the pipe.

kValues_turbulent.derivedExample: 3/4 in at Re 12,000: 90 ell K = 800/12000 + 0.4*(1+1/0.93) = 0.90; tee branch K = 1.49 -- consistent with Spears' 2.0 ft and 4.9 ft at f ~0.03 (K = f*Le/D = 0.77 and 1.9).

boreStandard.what: ASTM D2609 plastic insert fittings for PE pipe: MINIMUM inside diameter 'D' of the insert
boreStandard.note: These are MINIMUM bores; a given maker's fitting may be larger. Area ratio to SIDR pipe at the minimum bore: 1/2 0.43, 3/4 0.47, 1 0.51.

measuredLoss.found: No maker publishes a loss for barbed PE insert tees/ells/couplings. Nearest measurement: Bombardelli et al. 2019 (micro-irrigation connectors on 13 and 16 mm laterals) measured K_L from 2.72 to 24.16 (on lateral velocity), constant above Re 10,000, flow exponent ~2; the smallest K (2.72) was the near-coaxial union connector, the largest the one with a 1.56 diameter-ratio expansion.

derived.method: Sharp contraction into the D2609 minimum bore + sudden expansion out of it (both on bore velocity) + a turn loss at bore velocity (tee run 0.4, ell 0.75, tee branch 1.0) + Darcy friction over 3 in of bore; referred to pipe velocity by 1/beta^4. Water 60 F, smooth.

equivalentFtOfSamePE.note: range over 1-8 gpm; grows with flow because K is fixed while f falls

derived.crossCheck: Same order as PPFA's MEASURED PEX insert-fitting equivalents (1/2 in: elbow 9.4 ft, tee branch 10.4, tee run 2.4, coupling 2.0) and Bombardelli's K >= 2.7 for small barbed couplings; roughly 3x the solvent-weld PVC values. Couplings come out higher than PPFA's (crimp PEX couplings have a larger relative bore).
derived.caveat: Uses the D2609 MINIMUM bore; a real fitting with a larger bore loses much less (loss ~ 1/bore^4).

pex_insert_equivalentFt.what: PPFA/NAHB design guide, 'Consult manufacturer for other fitting friction losses'
pex_insert_equivalentFt.note: 'Long-radius tubing bends have the same head loss as straight tubing.'

copper_equivalentFt.what: Wrought copper (equivalent ft of straight tube)

values.rule: fittings = 10% of the PIPE FRICTION LOSS
values.where: Hunter handbook worked example: '0.28 PSI friction loss in fittings (estimate, 10% of friction loss in pipe)'

values.rule: 10%, 15% and up to 25% of mainline losses, or 30-50 pipe diameters of equivalent pipe
allow 10-20% pressure variation along a lateral (Hunter recommends 10%)

designerPractice.notFound: A rule stated as '10-20% of pipe LENGTH' was not found in a maker's guide; Hunter's is 10% of the pipe's friction LOSS (equivalent for straight runs). With insert fittings every few feet (barbed tees at each head on poly), 10% is far too low: one 3/4 in barbed tee branch is ~15-20 ft of pipe (derived above).

hunter_SJ.what: Hunter SJ Swing Joint (LIT-117 BR US 3/22): 0.49 in ID LDPE tubing, swivel ells both ends, 6 in or 12 in links, 1/2 or 3/4 in threads. ONE 'Swing joint friction loss' curve, not labelled by length or thread size.
hunter_SJ.readNote: Read by pixel-tracing the curve (+/- 0.15 psi). The curve's shape is odd for hydraulics: nearly linear below 4 gpm (loss ~ Q^1.1) and ~Q^1.6 above, where a fitting loss should go as ~Q^2 throughout. It may be a schematic drawing; use with doubt.

rainbird_SA.what: Rain Bird SA Series swing assemblies (6, 12, 18 in; 1/2 and 3/4 in; 0.490 in ID tubing): 'Pressure loss at 6 gpm (0.38 l/sec) is 2.0 psi'; 'Maximum flow is 8 gpm'. One figure for all lengths.

scaledByQsquared.note: scaled from the single published point as K*Q^2; the pipe part goes as Q^1.75-1.85, so low-flow values are slightly low.

rainbird_SPX_SB.what: Rain Bird SPX-FLEX swing pipe (0.487 in nominal ID) and SB spiral-barb fittings (SBE-050, SBE-075, SB-TEE, SB-CPLG): 80 psi, 8 gpm max. NO pressure-loss figure published.

hunter_HSBE_FLEXsg.what: Hunter HSBE-050/-075 spiral barb elbows and FLEXsg tubing (0.49 in ID), 80 psi. NO pressure-loss figure published.

toro_superFunnyPipe.what: Toro Super Funny Pipe friction loss, psi PER FOOT of pipe (no fittings)
toro_superFunnyPipe.disagreement: These are about HALF of H-W C=150 on a 0.49 in bore (2 gpm: 0.05 psi/ft computed vs 0.02 printed; 6 gpm: 0.38 vs 0.21). Toro's numbers would need a 0.55-0.59 in bore (or C ~ 200) to come out of H-W. Treat Toro's table as optimistic; use H-W/D-W on 0.49 in.

rainbird_TSJ_rigidPVC.what: Rain Bird TSJ turf swing joints (rigid PVC, swept elbows, 12 in), the three/four-elbow rotor style
rainbird_TSJ_rigidPVC.note: Rain Bird markets the swept elbows as lower-loss than competitors' sharp-cornered joints, so a field-built joint of standard street ells will lose more. TSJ-PRS (1 in) regulates to 70 psi and is 'not recommended' where lateral pressure is at or below the regulation pressure.

swingJoints.comparisonAt6gpm: Rain Bird SA (flexible, 0.49 in) 2.0 psi; Hunter SJ (flexible, 0.49 in, swivel ells) ~6.7 psi; Rain Bird TSJ 3/4 in rigid 0.3 psi. The two flexible assemblies differ by ~3x for nominally the same thing: the barb/swivel fitting bores (not published by anyone) dominate, not the tubing (12 in of 0.49 in tube at 6 gpm is ~0.4 psi).

designerPractice.rule: 'we figure 2.0 lbs. of pressure loss for these Funny Pipe swing joints' on sprays; never on rotors ('0.5 to 4.0 GPM through a 5/16 in hole... the barbed fittings are even smaller with a 1/4 in hole')
designerPractice.note: forum post (2017) quoted through a search snippet; landfx.com refused the fetch. The 5/16 in figure for the tube conflicts with the makers' 0.49 in ID; the 1/4 in barb bore is unverified.

designerPractice.rule: 1 in swing joint at ~11 gpm ~2.5 psi; typical 4 in pop-up rotor body ~5 psi, 6 in ~6 psi
designers 'would use a number of 1 or 2 psi for the swing-joint friction loss'
designerPractice.note: golf-course article; quoted via search snippet

threeElbowPVC_fieldBuilt.note: No maker chart. From Spears equivalents a 1/2 in Sch 40 joint of 3 x 90 ells (+ ~1 ft nipple) is ~5.5 ft of 1/2 in Sch 40: at 2 gpm ~0.10 psi, 4 gpm ~0.36, 6 gpm ~0.76 (H-W 150, ID 0.602). Threaded street ells have a smaller bore than solvent ells, so treat as a floor; 3/4 in ~4x less.

whereChartPressureIsQuoted.finding: 'All performance specifications are based on the stated working pressure available at the base of the sprinkler.' (Toro spec catalog pages for Mini 8, 300 Series and 640; the same sentence is on Toro's MPR Plus spray-nozzle sheet, which fits the 570Z.)

Charts say only 'Performance data derived from tests that conform with ASAE Standards; ASAE S398.1' and zero wind. But the same document's 'Flow Rate v Inlet Pressure' graph (no PRS) matches the table within ~2.5% (8.0 RC: table 5.90/7.06/8.03 gpm at 25/35/45 psi; graph ~5.7/6.85/7.83 at that INLET pressure), so the table pressure behaves as inlet (base) pressure.
No statement found on where the nozzle-chart pressure is taken. PRS spec language speaks of regulating 'the nozzle pressure'.

Charts label the column 'Pressure PSI' with no measurement point. For the PRB (regulated) rotor Hunter writes 'Nozzle discharge pressure: 45 PSI', i.e. the charts' 45 psi row is the nozzle pressure for a PRB.
LibreTexts defines P in q = 29.82 Cd D^2 sqrt(P) as 'pressure of the water at the inlet to the sprinkler device'.

sprinklerBodies.summary: Where stated (Toro) or inferable (Rain Bird 5000) the chart pressure is at the BASE/inlet of the head, so the body's internal loss is already inside the chart and must NOT be subtracted again. ASAE S398.1 / ISO 15886-3 set the actual tap location; their text was not accessible (ISO 15886-3:2021 notes it 'revised the pressure measurement method for pop-up sprinklers').

bodyInletLoss.found: No maker publishes a separate body/inlet loss for 1800, Pro-Spray, 570Z, 5000 or PGP. The only numbers are designers' allowances (4 in rotor ~5 psi, 6 in ~6 psi; landfx forum, practice) -- which double-count if the charts are at the base.

rainbird_1800_PRS.spec: 'The device shall regulate the nozzle pressure to 30 psi for inlet pressures from 35 to 70 psi. Below 35 psi the pressure loss shall not exceed 6 psi.' Product text: 'Regulates nozzle pressure to an average 30 psi with inlet pressures of up to 70 psi'; operating range 15-70 psi.
rainbird_1800_PRS.belowSetPoint: pass-through, loss <= 6 psi (a ceiling, not a curve)

rainbird_1800_P45.spec: 'regulate the nozzle pressure to 45 psi for inlet pressures from 50 to 70 psi. Below 50 psi the pressure loss shall not exceed 6 psi.'

rainbird_5000_PRS.chart: PRS table rows at 25/35/45 psi INLET are IDENTICAL to the non-PRS table (no pass-through loss assumed); the 55-75 psi band gives flows ~3.5% above the 45 psi row (8.0 RC 8.31 vs 8.03 gpm), i.e. a regulated nozzle pressure ~48 psi.

graphReading.note: Same document, 'Flow Rate v Inlet Pressure' graph, read by pixel tracing (+/- 1 psi). 8.0 RC: PRS flow below no-PRS by 9% at 20 psi, 8% at 30-45 psi -> equivalent pass-through loss ~3.6 psi at 4.5 gpm, ~4.8 at 5.8 gpm, ~5.7 at 6.8 gpm, ~6.3 at 7.3 gpm; regulation plateau (8.18 gpm) reached at ~55-60 psi inlet. 5.0 RC: curves coincide up to ~32 psi (no measurable loss at ~4 gpm), then ~2-4 psi in the 35-45 psi band as the regulator begins to close; plateau 5.0 gpm from ~52 psi.

rainbird_5000_PRS.disagreement: The 5000's own table (no loss below set point) and its own graph (3-6 psi loss) disagree. Rain Bird's 1800 spec (<= 6 psi) brackets both.

hunter_ProSpray_PRS30_PRS40.spec: 'Pressure-regulated to 30 PSI' / 'to 40 PSI'; 'Operational pressure range: 15 to 100 PSI'; catalog note: 'built-in pressure regulator controls output to a maximum of 30 PSI'.
hunter_ProSpray_PRS30_PRS40.belowSetPoint: not published ('maximum of 30 PSI' implies pass-through below)

hunter_PRB_rotor.spec: 'Pressure-regulated body (45 PSI)... (requires dynamic pressure differential: 15 PSI)'; 'Nozzle discharge pressure: 45 PSI'; 'Operating pressure range: 60 to 100 PSI' (2023 catalog); the web page says inlet '50-100 PSI'.
hunter_PRB_rotor.disagreement: 50 vs 60 psi minimum inlet in two Hunter documents; the stated 15 psi differential implies 60.

toro_570Z_PR.spec: 'In-stem... built-in pressure regulator... provides steady 30 PSI outlet pressure'; body operating range 20-75 psi (15-75 for LP models).

inlineRegulatorRule.rule: Hunter's inline regulators (PMR/ACZ): 'will maintain the predetermined operating pressure, provided that the inlet pressure is at least 5 PSI above the expected outlet pressure'.

modelSuggestion.rule: Below (set + ~5 psi for in-stem spray PRS; set + 15 psi for Hunter PRB rotors) treat the stem as pass-through: P_nozzle = P_inlet - dp, with dp ~ K*Q^2 bounded by Rain Bird's 6 psi spec; at spray flows (<= 4 gpm) the 5000 graph suggests dp of 0-3 psi. Above it, P_nozzle = set (Rain Bird 5000 data suggest ~set + 3 psi).

checkValves.note: SAM / CV drain-check options hold back 10-14 ft of head (Rain Bird SAM '14 feet... 6 psi'; Hunter CV 10 or 14 ft). They must be cracked open, an added opening pressure of ~4-6 psi; no flowing-loss figure is published.

nozzleFlowVsPressure.law: q = k * P^x with x = 0.5 for an orifice (turbulent jet). Sprinkler nozzles are treated as orifices in the textbooks and network software ('for nozzles and sprinkler heads the exponent on pressure is 0.5', Bentley WaterCAD); pressure-compensating devices have x near 0, laminar emitters near 1.

fittedToThisCatalogue.method: log-log least-squares slope of gpm vs psi for every nozzle with >= 3 charted pressures in water/lib/heads/*.json (2026-10-20); pressure-compensating families (Toro PSN/PCD, MPR Plus -PC) and the Rain Bird 5000 PRS inlet-indexed chart excluded.
fittedToThisCatalogue.examples: Rain Bird 5000 8.0 RC 25 -> 45 psi: x = 0.52; Rain Bird U-Series 0.50, MPR 0.50, HE-VAN 0.50; Hunter Pro fixed 0.53, MP Rotator 0.51, MP800 0.64; Toro PSN (pressure-compensating) 0.18; Rain Bird 5000 PRS by inlet 0.32.
fittedToThisCatalogue.reading: Charts are consistent with x = 0.5 to within rounding for sprays and rotors (median 0.52-0.53). The slight excess over 0.5 is what a base-referenced chart with a small internal loss (~Q^2) would produce. Use x = 0.5 to extrapolate; use the family's own fitted x if it differs by > 0.05.

validity.inside: Within the chart's printed pressure range the law is good to a few percent.
validity.outside: Not for pressure-compensating nozzles (x 0-0.35) or any PRS body above its set point (flow flat). Below the chart's lowest row the stream breaks up/radius collapses and the body may not pop up or seal (Rain Bird 1800 flow-by is 0 only at >= 8 psi; makers' minimum operating pressures 15-25 psi), so flow extrapolated below ~15 psi is unreliable. Above the top row misting changes radius, not flow; flow still follows x ~ 0.5 up to the body's maximum (70-100 psi). Keep extrapolation to about +/-20% beyond the chart's rows (speculation).

nozzleFlowVsPressure.minorLossExponent: Bombardelli et al. 2019 measured flow exponents ~2 for connector losses (dp ~ Q^2), consistent with fixed-K fitting losses.

notes: WHAT TO USE (recommendation, not a finding): PVC C=150 on the IA average ID; PE SIDR C=140 on the nominal ID (135 for 1/2 in); PEX C=150 on PPFA IDs; copper C=140 (130 old); galvanized C=120 new, 100 as the irrigation-chart design value, and lower for old pipe with no published curve; check small-pipe results against Darcy-Weisbach (smooth) which runs ~5-25% higher at residential flows.

Hard water and iron: no measured C-vs-time for PVC/PE/PEX in hard or iron-rich water was found. PVC in service 46 years measured C > 160 (municipal water). Galvanized ages fastest and also loses bore; the only age bands in print are for cast iron. Iron > 0.1-0.3 ppm and iron bacteria are documented as clogging emitters/nozzles (an IA paper: untreated 10 ppm-iron well lost 50-73% of drip flow in 18 days) rather than as a pipe C change.

Two ID conventions (IA average-wall vs OD - 2 x minimum wall) differ by ~0.02 in, worth ~10% of friction at 3/4 in. Rain Bird's own charts switched between them (2018 Class 200: 0.930; 2021 Sch 40: 0.804 average).

Swing joints are the largest single disagreement: at 6 gpm Rain Bird SA 2.0 psi vs Hunter SJ ~6.7 psi for the same 0.49 in tubing; Toro's per-foot table is about half of H-W. Nobody publishes the bore of a spiral-barb elbow.
Barbed insert fittings: only the ASTM D2609 MINIMUM bore is published; the derived losses assume it and are an upper bound for a fitting with a bigger bore.

Chart pressure is at the base/inlet where stated (Toro) or inferable (Rain Bird 5000); do not subtract a body loss from it. PRS stems below set point behave as pass-through with up to 6 psi loss (Rain Bird spec); Rain Bird's 5000 table assumes 0 loss and its graph shows 3-6 psi.

Units: every loss here is psi of water at ordinary temperature; 1 psi = 2.31 ft of head.
